title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
If you define robotics to be “embodied decision making”, then in many ways robotics *is* just a specific instantiating of AI. I disagree that robotics is in a winter - it’s a very pleasant spring right now in robot learning ☀️
Quoting @chr1sa
While AI is having a summer, robotics is stuck in winter. While the perception problems have been largely solved (thanks to AI), the other robotics problems -- understanding, planning, grasping, energy, flexibility, judgement, etc -- need breakthroughs.

Large open collaboration (BigScience, Eleuther, Stability) is wonderful to see in AI but the GLM-130B > BLOOM result suggests that steering and design decisions (ie. pretraining corpus) absolutely need to be strongly opinionated and correct. Easier to do this in smaller groups?

linked_urls.summary: Edit: This was cross posted to EA forum, and is a heavily downvoted post in their community. You can see the discussion here A lot has been talked about SBF/FTX/EA but this coverage reminds me that is time to talk about the toxicity of the culture within EA communities, especially as it relates to women. EA circles, much like the group house in Bahamas, are widely incestous where people mix their work life (in EA cause areas), their often polyamorous love life and social life in one amalgomous mix without strict separations.

OK, debates about the necessity or "priors" (or lack thereof) in learning systems are pointless.

What if you used LLMs for… all parts of RL?
GPT-4 as the Actor and Critic
GPT-4 as the Bellman Update
GPT-4 as the reward function
Vector DB as the replay buffer
GPT-4 as the importance sampling logic
Quoting @DrJimFan
What if we set GPT-4 free in Minecraft? ⛏️
I’m excited to announce Voyager, the first lifelong learning agent that plays Minecraft purely in-context. Voyager continuously improves itself by writing, refining, committing, and retrieving *code* from a skill library.
GPT-4 unlocks a new paradigm: “training” is code execution rather than gradient descent. “Trained model” is a codebase of skills that Voyager iteratively composes, rather than matrices of floats. We are pushing no-gradient architecture to its limit.
Voyager rapidly becomes a seasoned explorer. In Minecraft, it obtains 3.3× more unique items, travels 2.3× longer distances, and unlocks key tech tree milestones up to 15.3× faster than prior methods.

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
🚨Big things are happening in humanoid robotics!🚨
As we saw with drones and quadruped robots, it can take a mere decade for bleeding edge R&D areas to become "solved" platforms for commercial consumer use cases. Once open-ended research questions around reliability, dexterity, and cost have all been answered in a resounding fashion. Today, you can take your pick of low-cost stable consumer options that may have been impossible to imagine just 10 years ago.
And now, the writing is on the wall: the next few years will be transformative in bringing general-purpose humanoids from small scale proof-of-concept demos (ie. Atlas in the 2010s) to truly mature products available at scale.
2 notable recent announcements:
- Unitree H1 ( @UnitreeRobotics did for quadrupeds what DJI did for drones. Absolutely believable that Unitree can run it back and disrupt a new form of robots.
- AgiBot RAISE-A1 (
In case you aren't familiar with the founder 稚晖君 (Peng Zhihui), he is a legit 100x Engineer that recently left Huawei's prestigious "Youth Genius" program to start his own company, AgiBot. I've been following his amazing YouTube ( for a while now, and the proof is in the pudding: it seems that Peng is now only able to hack on full-stack robotics side projects, but also ship a real production robot. From inception to an on-stage demo of self-powered bipedal locomotion without support, it took less than 6 months.
These recent entrants join other humanoid players that I'm also particularly excited by:
- 1X EVE and NEO (
@1x_tech is well-positioned with a large head-start in building out an already impressive hardware platform and the buy-in of OpenAI. The long-term AI vision is led by my friend @ericjang11, whose prescient insight around generative modeling, imitation learning, and language-conditioning has influenced many research efforts to scale up smart robots, including those of my own team at Google DeepMind.
- Tesla Optimus (
@Tesla_AI impressed robotics experts with how quickly they went from marketing pitch to live hardware demo in less than a year. Once they reach some technological maturity, there are clear synergies with their existing supply chain and distribution know-how. The manipulation R&D efforts are in good hands (haha) with @julianibarz, my old manager responsible for creating the famous "Google Arm Farm"!
- Figure 01 (
@Figure_robot is one of the best-funded players led by a superstar founder @adcock_brett, who has a proven track record of shipping hard tech products (prev. @flyarcher). Long-term AI vision led by @corelynch, my old colleague whose keen research insight created a new subfield of learning from unstructured robot play data.
- Clone (
@clonerobotics is taking a unique approach with bio-memetic musculoskeletal humanoids. Big bet to swing for the fences, and led by the extremely sharp @dhanushisrad. When everyone else zigs, Clone zags.
There are a ton more cool humanoid efforts but these are the ones that I'm particularly excited by, thanks to their focus on building the Robot Brain and not just the Robot Body! Embodied AI is one of the most exciting challenges of our lifetimes, and I'm exceedingly optimistic about building it.

Quoting @davsca1
We are thrilled to share our groundbreaking paper published today in @Nature: "Champion-Level Drone Racing using Deep Reinforcement Learning." We introduce "Swift," the first autonomous vision-based drone that beat human world champions in several fair head-to-head races! PDF (open access): Video:
The "Swift" AI drone combines deep #reinforcementlearning in simulation with data collected in the physical world. This marks the first time that an autonomous mobile robot has beaten human champions in a real physical sport designed for and by humans. The key difference to previous achievements, like IBM’s Deep Blue winning against Gary Kasparov at chess in 1996 or Google DeepMind’s AlphaGo crushing the top champion Lee Sedol at Go in 2016, is that the previous feats were limited to board games or video games.
This work represents a milestone for mobile robotics, machine intelligence, and beyond, which may inspire the deployment of hybrid learning-based solutions in other physical systems, such as autonomous vehicles, aircraft, and personal robots, across a broad range of applications.
Kudos to my coauthors @kaufmann_elia @l_bauersfeld @antoniloq, the pilots @captainvanover @bmsthomas, and our supporters @m_schaepman @UZH_en @UZH_Science @UZHspacehub @ERC_Research @nccrrobotics

linked_urls.title: Champion-level drone racing using deep reinforcement learning | Nature
linked_urls.summary: First-person view (FPV) drone racing is a televised sport in which professional competitors pilot high-speed aircraft through a 3D circuit. Each pilot sees the environment from the perspective of their drone by means of video streamed from an onboard camera. Reaching the level of professional pilots with an autonomous drone is challenging because the robot needs to fly at its physical limits while estimating its speed and location in the circuit exclusively from onboard sensors1. Here we introduce Swift, an autonomous system that can race physical vehicles at the level of the human world champions. The system combines deep reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation with data collected in the physical world. Swift competed against three human champions, including the world champions of two international leagues, in real-world head-to-head races. Swift won several races against each of the human champions and demonstrated the fastest recorded race time. This work represents a milestone for mobile robotics and machine intelligence2, which may inspire the deployment of hybrid learning-based solutions in other physical systems. An autonomous system is described that combines deep reinforcement learning with onboard sensors collecting data from the physical world, enabling it to fly faster than human world champion drone pilots around a race track.

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
Announcing Open X-Embodiment! One of the most ambitious and large-scale robot learning collaborations to date.
Intelligent robots have seen tremendous progress the past years by leveraging big real-world datasets, high capacity network architectures, and transfer from web-scale foundation models. BUT! One tricky open challenge has been how to effectively leverage data from many robots and demonstrate downstream control capabilities to many robots. In fact, most projects today -- whether in industry or in academic labs -- will start data collection and algorithm design from (almost) scratch because the status quo has been that (1) there just isn't enough overlap between existing datasets and your specific problem domain, and (2) the plumbing required to try to shoehorn other datasets into your learning pipeline is just too hard and not worth the effort.
And that's where Open X-Embodiment comes in!
A truly unprecedented collaboration with over 170 authors across 34 research labs, Open X-Embodiment aims to address both challenges (1) and (2) via a huge open-sourced cross-embodiment dataset, plug-and-play data infrastructure, model checkpoints, and initial de-risking that shows these diverse datasets actually transfer some amount of new capabilities directly to your robot setup!
It's likely that the specific robot platform and the types of semantic tasks you care about are already contained in the dataset. And unlike prior definitive works on cross-embodiment datasets like the amazing RoboNet, Open X-Embodiment focuses on huge datasets that prioritize high-quality (demonstrations) and diverse (tons of tasks and environments) behaviors.
...so does all this data actually help? We find that indeed, we see positive transfer when training on multiple datasets compared to just training on a single dataset! We find that RT-1-X, an RT-1 model trained on cross-embodiment datasets, is able to outperform single-dataset baselines (including those tuned for the specific robot setups). Yes, that's right: a single multi-robot policy is able to run directly on different robot embodiments in different labs around the world, showing impressive performance gains!
But do we actually need so much physical real-world robotics data? Will getting more internet data get us all this transfer for free? To answer this question, we introduce RT-2-X: an RT-2 model (a vision-language-action model that directly predicts actions as language!) that is trained on both internet data as well as the Open X-Embodiment datasets. Indeed, we see that RT-2-X is able to now understand a few emergent capabilities like spatial relationships a lot better than the RT-2 model that didn't see all the new cross-robot data. So, it seems like non-embodied internet data may not be enough, at least for now: there is still a very critical role for real world robot interaction datasets!
I hope this release and the initial exploratory results are as inspiring for you as they are for me! I believe that we've entered a new world of possibilities for exploring data-driven embodied intelligence that’s powered by a continual open community collaboration. I’m excited to see what great progress we’ll make together on pushing the frontiers of cross-embodiment learning forward.
There are WAY too many collaborators to thank, so please see the website for the full list of authors!

(2) On the surface, it may look like learning correlations in text, but it turns out that to 'just learn' statistical correlations in text, to compress information really well, what the neural network learns is some representation of the process that produced the text.
(3) This text is a projection of the world...what the neural network is learning is aspects of the world, of people, of the human conditions, their hopes, dreams, motivations, their interactions...the situations we are in. The neural network learns a compressed, abstract, usable representation."

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
We’re living through the golden age of AI Research:
- Highly leveraged impact thanks to successful methods scaling and transferring easily to other domains (ie. generative modeling ideas landing in language, robotics, representation learning)
- Relatively low ramp-up cost due to how fast the field is moving. A motivated undergrad with 1-2 years of focused study/building can likely already start making non-trivial research contributions. Compare this to fields which require 10+ years of formal training just to get started (ie. theoretical physics)
- So many non-traditional research opportunities: open science collaborations (from Eleuther to /r/LocalLlama), AI startups that don’t gatekeep on pedigree, new career options such as residencies or RE tracks. Optimizing for metrics like h-index is still possible, but there are now so many more options that are just as valuable if not more. Research is increasingly moving faster than traditional peer-review cycles support: workshop whitepapers, pre-prints, and model releases drive the bleeding edge every week.
Quoting @_aidan_clark_
Seeing people tweet about doing PhD apps and I’ll just say I got into 0/8 of the programs I applied to and things turned out great. There are lots of opportunities for research, don’t stress :)

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
AI as Universal Computation
I've been admiring a research perspective for a while now that seeks to draw direct parallels between learning algorithms and general computing paradigms.
This purposeful framing compares current and future trends in scaling neural networks with corresponding ideas in computing. It's not merely a one-off heuristic, but rather a core driving motivation (faith, if you will) determining the most impactful directions.
This mentality is evident in foundational AI advancements, such as data/model parallelism, specialized tokens and registers, power scaling laws, compression/quantization, and MapReduce-like decoding mechanisms.
More recently, it's fascinating to witness this belief system in action regarding the progress on State Space Models (SSMs). The "Recurrent vs. Convolutional" views of SSMs explicitly illustrate the tradeoff between time and memory ( But these metaphors can be extended to nearly any paradigm that has demonstrated scalability in AI.
One organization that seems to fully embrace this mindset is OpenAI. Much of their research agenda revolves around the concept of AI as Universal Computation, and they've developed algorithms and methods accordingly.

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
"Google is washed" "It's so over for Google lmao" "Google can only do research and can't ship"
The bull case for Google winning the AI Wars has some historic precedent: the trends seen in Speech R&D. In 2014, after years of a seemingly comfortable Google R&D lead, an upstart Amazon Alexa came out of left field and shocked the world with impressive speech models shipped in a product. For a while, critics of Google pronounced the death of Google Speech R&D moats, pointing to shipped Google speech features as underwhelming in the face of Alexa.
But... Google got its shit together, and over the next 4 years, consistently shipped a plethora of both research and product breakthroughs, once again claiming a widening lead by leveraging end-to-end seq2seq models for speech recognition and generation (see: [1] [2] and countless other works). Today, both researchers and consumers view Google's speech capabilities as some of the best.
The parable of the Speech Wars does not map 1:1 to the [coming] AI Wars, but certain parallels do apply. I think many would reject the premise that Google DeepMind was ever "behind" in terms of capabilities and research, but for those who believe that: I expect the landscape of externally accessible AI models, products, and capabilities to vastly change in the coming months and years. I can't speak publicly about any specifics, but I am really looking forward to what's coming!

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
“Sora doesn’t show any new technical innovations” - this take misses the point. 🎯
Sora (and other great polished OAI releases) are not *meant* to provide new knowledge to the research community. They are not papers, careful scientific experiments, or theory that adds to the sum of AI research. They are scaled up systems that are meant to convince the *public* that the utility and arrival of A(G)I are eminent.
AI researchers complaining that “of course we knew that Diffusion Transformers + huge batch sizes + patches across time can scale! of course video game engines can provide good synthetic pretraining data!” are often those deep in the weeds: seeing results, adjusting their internal priors, and searching for new problems to work on.
But finding new problems and new algorithms to solve them is not what OAI’s public systems releases aim to do!
Do I wish OAI participated more in open science? Yes.
Do I appreciate the empirical results of what massive scaling + high quality engineering can enable? Also yes.
So: kudos to the Sora team for a well-executed model and what was most definitely a crazy engineering effort, and kudos to the pioneers in the generative video and diffusion space whose research was the basis for Sora! 🎥

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
I can’t emphasize enough how mind-blowing extremely long token context windows are. For both AI researchers and practitioners, massive context windows will have transformative long-term impact, beyond one or two flashy news cycles. ↔️
“More is different”: Just as we saw emergent capabilities when scaling model size, compute, and datasets, I think we’re going to see a similar revolution for in-context learning. The capability shifts we’ll see going from 8k to 32k to 128k to 10M (!!) token contexts and beyond are not just going to be simple X% quantitative improvements, but instead qualitative phase shifts which unlock new abilities altogether and result in rethinking how we approach foundation model reasoning.
Great fundamental research on the relationship between in-context learning (ICL) and in-weight learning is now more relevant than ever, and needs to be extended given that we now operate in an era where the "X-axis" of context length has increased by three orders of magnitude. I highly recommend @scychan_brains's pioneering work in this area, such as and In fact, there are already data points which suggest our understanding of ICL scaling laws still contains large gaps🤔(see
Also exciting is the connection of long-context ICL to alignment and post-training! I'm curious to see how 10M+ contexts disrupt the ongoing debate about whether foundation models truly learn new capabilities and skills during finetuning/RLHF or whether they purely learn stylistic knowledge (the "Superficial Alignment Hypothesis", and The Gemini 1.5 technical report brings new evidence to this discussion as well, showing that an entire new language can be learned completely in context. I'm excited to see better empirical understanding of how foundation models can effectively leverage large-context ICL both during inference but also for "learning to learn" during training
And finally, perhaps the most important point: huge context lengths will have a lasting impact because their applications are so broad. There is no part of modern foundation model research that is not changed profoundly in some capacity by huge contexts! From theoretical underpinnings (how we design pre-training and post-training objectives) to system design (how we scale up long-contexts during training and serving) to application domains (such as robotics), massive context ICL is going to have significant impact and move the needle across the board.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GHNlSo1aoAA9zbe.jpg

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
“LLMs can not feel emotions and are therefore not alive” is ill-posed.
LLMs have been trained on lifetimes of raw, passionate, diverse expressions of human emotion, both fictionalized and real — from dramatic Hollywood screenplays, from wistful memoirs written from deathbeds, from intimate inner thoughts recorded in private journals, from great epics of sorrow and tragedy penned by humanity’s greatest artists.
LLMs have seen more of the human condition than you or I will ever know in our lifetimes. Lived qualia may be indispensable for an anthropocentric experience of the world, but if you solely want to judge consciousness as the ability to interpret and invoke emotion, then LLMs may meet that bar already.
That being said, this bar is ill-posed, and Gemini/Claude 3/GPT-4 are indeed not alive 🤔

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
I often see an incomplete modern interpretation of the Bitter Lesson.
Simple methods which scale effectively don’t win by outperforming competing methods (which may be more theoretically compelling) on scientific merit alone. Perhaps more important than algorithmic optimality, *economics* plays a large role in the dominance of big models + big data.
At the core of the Bitter Lesson is an unshakeable emphasis on scaling up simple methods which will predictably improve with more parameters, more data, and more FLOPS. This stands in stark contrast to the prevailing paradigm in many other areas of technological capabilities research, where R&D often spend a significant or even majority of resources on the innovation required to figure out how to adapt a proof-of-concept algorithm to larger production scales. Then, one of the most important properties of Bitter Lesson-esque scaling may actually be an economic insight: that one can take open-ended unbounded R&D risk (in terms of capital, time, and human labor) and turn it into an engineering challenge (hard but bounded).
In other words, the Bitter Lesson claims that methods which exhibit good Elasticity of Capabilities with respect to Engineering will outperform methods which do not. “Expensive but tractable” is a very difficult baseline to beat!

If you work on AI or enjoy hard sci-fi, I highly recommend “Permutation City” by Greg Egan — it’s an astoundingly imaginative treatise that’s more relevant than ever today, in an era of foundation models compressing / simulating the sum of human knowledge.

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
Prompts as PsyOps: 2 million surgically crafted multimodal tokens of *anything* meant to steer foundation models towards a good region of latent space. But the *anything* need not be interpretable nor based on human priors; in fact, anthropomorphizing models may be fundamentally limiting 👽
For a given task, it’s possible that the optimal context might be any combination of any set of tokens; we’ve found a few strong patterns (ie. Chain of Thought) but are far from solving the context construction problem, if a general “solution” even exists.
There are many ways to view context construction: prompt engineering, priming (explicit or covert), circuit activation, multi-turn dialogue (“just ask for X”), cognitive calibration, meta-learning via in-context learning, and so on. One can argue that these framings all successfully leverage inductive biases from human cognition as a strong basis for concepts that transfer well to foundation model contexts. Exemplar-based contexts provide structure, style, and relevant prior data; contexts which are closer to data distributions seen during training allow better transfer/interpolation from pretraining capabilities.
…but there is actually no inherent reason why an anthropomorphic approach is necessary or sufficient for the most powerful foundation model contexts! We can already see this in initial successes from variety of approaches which give up expert-based heuristics. Two examples:
1) All retrieval-style methods embrace a data driven approach to context construction. Just retrieve relevant information, potentially based solely on distance measures in some abstract latent space. Smoosh together context from different modalities, different sources, different qualities: if the latent space says the context is useful, it gets added.
2) Gradient based approaches (ie. GCG literally just run backprop against input tokens in order to optimize for tokens most likely to produce desired outputs. Prompts personalized based on frozen weights from a particular LLM often transfer to other LLMs.
…but even if we only consider context construction approaches based on human priors, there’s still a ton of diversity within human approaches to persuasion. Anything that’s worked for social engineering at micro scales or for psyops at macro scales are reasonable approaches to human-interpretable context construction (

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
🚨In case you missed it: it’s been non-stop technical progress updates from Chinese humanoid companies the past 48 hours! 🚨
In just the last 2 days, batched updates from numerous exciting Chinese humanoid companies all dropped at once:
1) @UnitreeRobotics showcases technical improvements bringing the low-cost G1 humanoid robot closer and closer to a platform ready to scale for mass production. Seems like there are significant mechatronic and stability improvements, with progress also made on their end-to-end vision based sim2real RL stack for bipedal locomotion. No surprises at all that Unitree is showcasing impressive (and possibly state of the art) mobility capabilities, given their deep experience in rapidly commercializing quadruped locomotion in the past.
Source:
2) AGIBot ( announces five commercial bi-arm robots, with substantial progress in scaling up a teleoperation-based data engine, VLM-based planning and control policies, and whole-body mobile manipulation. I really like their north star vision of integrating foundation models (LLMs and VLMs) into the embodied intelligence stack; actions are just another modality. Of course, talk is cheap and execution is everything, but I like the ambition of going out there and trying to tackle the entire full-stack of AI + Robotics.
Source:
3) Astribot ( unveils the new build of their bimanual wheeled robot, S1. Very impressed by their smooth autonomous trajectories in a variety of fairly precise manipulation tasks! Going solely off of the recent Chinese humanoid demo videos, I think Astribot is likely leading on their manipulation learning stack. The platform and choice of tasks/demo reminds me a lot of 1X’s autonomy update from earlier this year (

...and what about the west? American humanoid companies made significant progress earlier this year, with sneak peaks of new hardware platforms (ie. @Figure_robot 02 and @TheSanctuaryAI Phoenix initial pilot deployment teasers (ie. @Tesla_Optimus in factories and technical learning stack previews (ie. @1x_tech
And while American industrial humanoid news was relatively quite the last months, fundamental humanoid research progressed in academia, with advances in human-to-humanoid teleoperation (ie. OpenTelevision and whole-body control HumanPlus
It’s great to see the rapid pace of innovation for humanoid robots globally. What’s especially interesting is that we’re starting to see the results of compounding early differences between companies across hardware, software, and business strategy. While a year ago almost all companies were showcasing stiff prototype hardware waddling around or performing rudimentary rigid pick and place tasks, today’s demos showcase a much wider array of design choices – from agile bipedal robots, autonomous household consumer tasks, and substantial embodiment design differences. Demos are also noticeably more polished, seem slightly less hacky, and definitely one step closer to scalable products. Progress is fast!
But I’m still not seeing mature demonstrations of either (1) dexterous control more complex end-effectors than parallel jaw grippers and (2) robust and steerable generalization similar to what consumers are used to for LLMs. I’m looking forward to seeing how robotics researchers and humanoid companies can push on one or both of these axes in the coming months!

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
The field of Robotics + AI is at a very interesting moment in time right now because we’re seeing the evolution of how optimism from the last 10 years of research is carrying over to new frontiers: towards commercialization, towards more complex morphologies and applications, towards dreams of generality usually reserved for “AGI research”.
There are now big questions around how historic trends will project onto the current robotics + AI wave. How applicable are the cyclical patterns we’ve seen play out in frontier modeling? In RL + search? In AV commercialization? In agent/code GenAI? In SaaS customer flywheels? In hardware startups tackling integration challenges?
But more interesting is that there are even big questions around how actual *robotics research* applies to these new frontiers! There’s been a lot of exciting progress in the last years on training large multitask robot policies, on sim2real policy learning, on fleet-scale robot data collection, on learning robust and generalizable policies — but most of this research targeted embodiments and application complexities that are substantially simpler than where goalposts are today with complex manipulation, humanoids, and commercial production requirements.
I think this last point is especially important and undervalued. A lot of folks new to robot learning are assuming that the same scaling laws and approaches that have worked elsewhere will easily be applied in robotics: self-play in AlphaGo, world model learning in video generation, sim2real in locomotion, search in CodeGen/math, exploration in Minecraft. These are indeed very promising and exciting research areas, but my main advice when asked about these directions is that robotics has a very different set of operating constraints and comparative challenges than other domains.
Moravec’s Paradox applies to technical algorithms as well: what methods excel at in one domain they may struggle with in robotics, and where methods face challenges in other domains they may scale better in robotics.

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
Action-conditioned world models are one step closer! Neural simulations hold a lot of promise for scaling up real-world interaction data, especially for domains which physics-based simulators struggle at. 🚀
Quoting @_akhaliq
Google presents Diffusion Models Are Real-Time Game Engines
discuss:
We present GameNGen, the first game engine powered entirely by a neural model that enables real-time interaction with a complex environment over long trajectories at high quality. GameNGen can interactively simulate the classic game DOOM at over 20 frames per second on a single TPU. Next frame prediction achieves a PSNR of 29.4, comparable to lossy JPEG compression. Human raters are only slightly better than random chance at distinguishing short clips of the game from clips of the simulation. GameNGen is trained in two phases: (1) an RL-agent learns to play the game and the training sessions are recorded, and (2) a diffusion model is trained to produce the next frame, conditioned on the sequence of past frames and actions. Conditioning augmentations enable stable auto-regressive generation over long trajectories.

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
Ilya once said that when super-human world modeling is achieved, robotics would be solved 6 months later: just solve AGI, and then ask the AGI to solve robotics.
But is this plausible given current trends? 🤔
Today’s SOTA frontier models soak up human-centric priors represented in human-generated internet; probably good for language, but potentially bad for robots. If future frontier model training relies critically on things like YouTube and first-person human videos, then it may be expected that the latent knowledge contained within future models will be heavily biased towards physical interactions which are natural to humans for the human form factor.
But this goes beyond just the exterior shape of the robot (“two arms, two legs, ten fingers”), but also the entire kinematic profile of how the robot makes contact with the world. The contact dynamics distribution shift may be the most important factor in the human2robot embodiment gap!
My own take: I would agree that *if* you believe that AGI will overfit to an anthropomorphic perspective of interaction, then the human to robot gap needs to be solved by hardware. But! I think it may be possible for frontier models to learn a universal world model that disentangles natural physics from human-based interaction. At some abstraction level, there’s just one true platonic representation of the physical world; how humans choose to shape that world is just one small part of the platonic representation. Sure, this one part is the most abundantly represented in 2024 internet datasets, but that doesn’t mean that it will be intractable to make progress towards learning the true universal physics world model, which is not specific to human-based modes of interacting with the world.
Highly recommend @ericjang11’s new post around robot motors, reflected inertia, safety, and what it means for AI

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
Promising progress from 1X on learned world models which improve with more experience and physical interaction data.
What I'm excited about:
- World models are likely the only path forward for reproducible and scalable evaluations in *multi-agent settings*; see success of world model evals for AV.
- Building world models off of 2024 technology (GENIE, VideoPoet) is a few orders of magnitude easier than early 2023 technology.
- Once world models are good enough for evaluation, they are likely already at least 90% of the way there for training on as well.
Open challenges:
- How do you get the correct data distributions to train a robust world modeler (which can capture the long tail of real world failure modes) without first collecting real world data of those failure modes? All good policies are good in the same ways, but all bad policies are each bad in their own unique ways.
- Related to the previous point, is there a minimum scale of real-world data you need before it makes sense to start training a world model? Is world modeling something you always distill a backlog of real-world interaction into, or can you make a "predictive" world model which can actually generalize?
- Evaluations are especially valuable for measuring out-of-distribution scenarios. World models make a bet that it will be easier to model the compounding effects of OOD trajectories than it is to learn OOD action prediction.
Super excited to see more works along this direction!

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
Pi_0 release is very exciting, congrats to the whole team!
Great progress on a generalist robot foundation model with two new VLA models, showcased on different dexterous bi-manual platforms.
Some quick thoughts, any corrections are welcome if you have more information:
- Really nice to see high zero-shot success rates for in-distribution training tasks, even exceeding 80% for some tasks.
- A compute-parity ablation is a nice way to try to fairly compare the tradeoffs between more performant VLA backbones vs. higher resource cost of pre-training and finetuning. It's clear that going from even "Pi_0-small" to "Pi_0 (parity)", there is some gain for scaling up!
- As we have continually seen with robot foundation models, hierarchy is quite helpful for more complex tasks, since episode-level instructions ("fold the laundry") require the VLA to do both low-level control learning but also high-level semantic reasoning. In contrast, providing more granular commands or plans (in this case, in 2 second windows) can perhaps alleviate the amount of implicit planning the VLA needs to do. It is great to see first steps from recent works (RT-H, Embodied CoT) start to make their way publicly into dexterous long-horizon settings. Caveat: the intermediate language used here seem to be quite coarse still, at the abstraction level of just object pick/place locations.
- The post-training results in Pi_0 are a little mixed, in my opinion. On an absolute scale, Pi_0 finetuning to both in-distribution and OOD tasks seems pretty good. However, the finetuning scaling results for "Pi_0 (scratch)" are not that much worse than "Pi_0"! This suggests that while Pi's robot foundation model pretraining stage (ie. OXE, cross-embodied bimanual demos) is adding some boost to finetuning performance, most of the gains come from the architecture itself (PaliGemma + tokenization scheme + flow matching). Would love to be corrected if my intepretation is faulty!

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
Robotics + AI has completely transformed: a perfect storm of AI breakthroughs, hardware innovation, and capital inflow. But are general robot foundation models truly just around the corner?
At recent talks, I took an honest look at hype vs. reality to share what’s missing 🧵👇
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/ext_tw_video_thumb/1869906356268109824/pu/img/512pAhM5kBs-ltzG.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/ext_tw_video/1869906356268109824/pu/vid/avc1/480x270/gvjJ5hCnvrb06voW.mp4?tag=12

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
I’ve gradually come around to two paths to embodied AGI that I was very skeptical of before:
1️⃣ solving robotics via reasoning
2️⃣ solving robotics via world modeling
I was previously doubtful not of these approaches themselves, but of timelines and efficiency; the “optimal” algorithms or approaches to use may not be the ones which make the most progress. Hardware and software lotteries are very real, especially in robotics where prohibitive CapEx and OpEx limit the search space of research ideas. So when trillions of dollars and millennia of R&D hours of effective investment have been poured into pre-training, scaling, and inference optimization for internet-scale LLMs, this is a powerful foundation to build off, and a very tough baseline ecosystem to beat — even if suboptimal for something like robotics.
But recent progress and momentum in reasoning and generative world modeling give me hope that we’ll see alternative approaches to unlocking general-purpose robotics, with competitive pace of progress! More entropy is better when we are still so early.
Two directions I would love to see more signals on in 2025:
1️⃣ For reasoning / search-based models, to show that inference-time compute scaling can be amortized and distilled into training. While minutes (hours?!) of thinking processes might make sense in return for very strong results in coding or math, this is simply a non-starter in real world robotics. Additionally, I would love to see evidence of how well “thinking harder” improves physical embodied reasoning performance. The types of intelligence required for low-level control are very different than the types of intelligence required for solving math Olympiad problems or debugging large software codebases.
2️⃣ For generative world modeling, to show that the important physical properties of the world are modeled in a non-trivial manner. Beyond basic concepts like object permanence or the forward arrow of time, how well do approaches like action-conditioned video prediction (which are generally optimized for *aesthetic reconstruction*, rather than physical grounding) capture the details of what’s important for robotic control? I would like to see how world models capture different behavior modes, capture different levels of optimality (model not only successful world interactions, but also failures), and different robot embodiments (assumptions valid in for a factory robot may be very bad for modeling home robots).
The future is bright! For both 1️⃣ and 2️⃣, progress is orders of magnitudes what we saw in 2023. Looking forward to an even more diverse and interesting 2025 ⭐️
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/1872392515107926016/img/rGS-PzgdITLI9A66.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/1872392515107926016/vid/avc1/480x270/KyEAnSFWhtlYq5om.mp4?tag=16

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
Extremely saddened to hear about Felix’s passing. His thoughtful research contributions played a major part of my own development as a scientist.
Most recently, his poignant essay on AI and stress humanized the pressure cooker that is today’s AI environment. It resonated deeply with me and many other AI researchers, and said out loud the undercurrent of what it has been like to live through immense amounts of change in a career that almost overnight transformed from open-ended curiosity driven science to a hyper-scaled arms race where the stakes feel overwhelming.
The stars have aligned and it seems that if you play your cards right, have enough agency, be “cracked” enough… there is an unreasonably high likelihood of outsized impact on the world, acquiring generational wealth, becoming a household name, or all of the above. None of these were original motivations for any of us to start working on AI/RL/language/robotics. But since such a path seems *possible*, one seems almost *obligated* to try to take advantage and live up to this rarest of opportunities: to contribute to the arrival of AGI with your entirety, at the cost of almost everything else.
It is both comforting but also a bit sad that my brightest friends (much more accomplished than myself) also feel this way - be it at AGI labs, at flashy billion dollar startups, at tenure-track faculty positions.
I don’t really have a good rebuttal to this internalized stress/FOMO. Standard platitudes like “comparison is the thief of joy” or “just do good work and the rest will fall into place” seem stale in the face of countless examples of peers who are indeed navigating the rising stakes of AI with urgency, with strategy, and concrete life-altering results to show for it. I am still thinking through a lot of this, and if you have any answers or thoughts, please share.
I hope that we can still remember that behind every hype, every amazing paper, every model release, every fundraise: we are all human beings and can treat each other with kindness and care. In the grand scheme of things, what we will recall fondly 50 years from now is that we had the amazing opportunity to work on AGI together, the most miraculous human-made technology up until that point.
RIP Felix — you will be missed. Thank you for your research leadership and your inspiration for everyone in AI to think more thoughtfully about themselves and peers not just as researchers, but also as human beings.

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
A lot of interesting discussion recently on the implications of OpenAI being a major sponsor of the FrontierMath benchmark.
There are two extremes of what this implies:
1) omg OAI is benchmark hacking and leaking test data into training!
2) OAI uses questions in the private FrontierMath to inform the high-level design and goals when creating new training datasets / reasoning traces.
Of course, there are also options in between these two extremes, such as slightly rephrasing questions into a new training dataset so that *technically* the test tokens were never trained on.
But the stakes are really high for frontier models when the competition is so fierce. Models that use these tricks will have artificially high benchmark scores, and absolutely fail to generalize to other domains outside of the benchmarks. Frontier labs can not afford these kind of games, which why I believe OpenAI uses FrontierMath more for option 2) above. Don’t get me wrong — this is still a pretty large undisclosed detail, and it definitely means that o1 and o3 performance on FrontierMath (relative to other frontier models) will be higher than their performance on hard reasoning domains which were not optimized for during training dataset design. But I don’t think the results will look some of the tiny LLMs which have done option 1) on benchmarks on MMLU, where there’s a night and day difference between benchmark numbers and the vibes of the model’s general capabilities.
For those who really think OpenAI did option 1) and leaked training data — I’d wait to see o3’s *relative* reasoning performance on production use cases and other benchmarks compared to the next generation of thinking frontier models. It will be interesting to see whether o3 wins most / loses least on FrontierMath.

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
The next Figure autonomy update is finally out, with some new demos and nice technical details on how they're combining Vision-Language-Action Models with humanoids. Some thoughts below🤔
What I liked: ⭐️
- Decoupling the control frequency of a slower, larger model (7B param "System 2 VLM" at 7-9Hz) from the control frequency of a faster, reactive model (80M "System 1" at 200Hz, probably with action chunking) is a very nice approach in a day and age where specialist single-task small models (ACT, Diffusion Policy) are working reasonably well for high-DoF hardware systems.
- Upper-torso control unlocks a much larger effective workspace than tabletop-only manipulation, and the videos show nice behaviors with good range of motion, such as reaching above the head for the top level of the refrigerator.
- The sample efficiency for learning this multitask humanoid policy seems on par with much simpler one-armed systems. 500 hours of teleoperated demos is roughly on par (same order of magnitude) as the pick and place demonstration data for RT-2, even though the Figure humanoid upper torso + hands is a much more complex system.
- There is some positive transfer from "VLM knowledge" to low-level control, with demos of instructions that require understanding visual-language semantics. This is expected for VLA models, but a good sign nonetheless that Figure's VLA training stack is doing reasonable things.
What I look forward to in the future: 📈
- All tasks shown were relatively simple pick and place skills. While the demos show 35-DoF control in a stable manner, the full potential of bi-manual dexterity is not tested at all. Achieving both dexterity and generalization has been *the* fundamental challenge that no humanoid company has shown any signs of life on, and this release is unfortunately no different.
- Despite 200Hz upper torso commands being sent from the System 1, motions still seem a bit jerky, and look like they could be accomplished with <50Hz. This likely suggests that the hardware/firmware stack for Figure has a much higher level of polish than the autonomy.
Overall, I am impressed by the end-to-end execution of the release. It's a big step up from the technical update we saw last year, and a strong testament to the maturing full stack prowess from the whole Figure team! Congrats to @coreylynch @YevgenChebotar and co, I look forward to seeing more in the future!

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
Great to see the latest intelligence update from the NVIDIA GR00T team on building a robot foundation model for humanoids! I just went through a deep read of the technical report and have some initial thoughts 👇
What I liked:
- This is the first open-weights humanoid VLA foundation model, and very accessible at just 2B. The whole ecosystem (model and infra) will likely be great for the developer community. I'm looking forward to seeing all the great research that will build off of it in the coming months!
- I have followed Yuke's vision of a data pyramid for a few years now, and this is one of the largest scale efforts to realize the combination of internet data, synthetic data, and real-world robot data. This is no easy feat, and kudos to the team on integrating so many moving pieces: Cosmos video generation, RoboCasa simulation with DexMimicGen, GR-1 real-world teleop, cross-embodiment VLA training, and high-DoF diffusion policy with upper body control.
- Scaling up a learned latent action model to align the actions of not just simple tabletop robots but also humanoids is nice to see.
- The real-world tasks go beyond pick-and-place -- some pouring, and some articulated objects. Still not "dexterous" but better than top down picking.
- The VLA finetuning objective uses object detection as an auxiliary loss. Cool to see that general spatial understanding is an important capability to retain during robot training!
What I'm looking forward to next:
- My expectation going into the paper was that this work would answer the question of what the role of synthetic data is for real-world humanoid manipulation. I am not fully convinced by these initial results; the experimental baselines ablate over modeling choices, but strikingly do not discuss the benefits of adding synthetic data. Adding simulated data or neural trajectories (generated videos labeled with synthetic actions using a learned IDM) is a key contribution of this work, so I am disappointed there are no ablations showing the impact of these data sources in either pre-training or post-training.
- The power of VLAs is to enable robust generalization; I had hoped to see more coverage of generalization in the quantitative evaluations.
- On the VLA algorithm side, prior works have found that co-fine-tuning robotics data alongside internet data is important. However, N1 freezes the VLM backbone, so it's unclear how much positive transfer is coming from the VLM vs. just acting as a pretty good pre-trained representation.
Overall, I am quite impressed with the end-to-end execution and the progress since the last updates, which focused on completely different aspects (locomotion, whole-body control, sim2real). Awesome to see manipulation getting some love -- the most challenging bottleneck for solving robotics! Congrats to the whole GR00T team 👏
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GmXai6IawAAW7BS.jpg
Quoting @DrJimFan
Excited to announce GR00T N1, the world’s first open foundation model for humanoid robots! We are on a mission to democratize Physical AI. The power of general robot brain, in the palm of your hand - with only 2B parameters, N1 learns from the most diverse physical action dataset ever compiled and punches above its weight:
- Real humanoid teleoperation data.
- Large-scale simulation data: we are open-sourcing 300K+ trajectories!
- Neural trajectories: we apply SOTA video generation models to “hallucinate” new synthetic data that features accurate physics in pixels. Using Jensen’s words, “systematically infinite data”!
- Latent actions: we develop novel algorithms to extract action tokens from in-the-wild human videos and neural generated videos.
GR00T N1 is a single end-to-end neural net, from photons to actions:
- Vision-Language Model (System 2) that interprets the physical world through vision and language instructions, enabling robots to reason about their environment and instructions, and plan the right actions.
- Diffusion Transformer (System 1) that “renders” smooth and precise motor actions at 120 Hz, executing the latent plan made by System 2.
We deploy N1 on GR1 robot, 1X Neo robot, and a large collection of simulation benchmarks. N1 achieves up to +30% boost in diverse manipulation tasks for household and industrial settings.
While humanoid robots are the main focus of N1, our model also supports cross-embodiment. We finetune it to work on the $110 HuggingFace LeRobot SO100 robot arm! Open robot brain runs on open hardware. Sounds just right.
Let’s solve robotics, together, one token at a time.

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
There are definitely a ton of areas where GDM can improve in! But two points make me overall quite optimistic about GDM still:
1) There are technology areas where GDM is still quite far ahead of all external competitors, both AGI labs as well as startups. To many, it's very meaningful to be on the bleeding edge and working on answers to questions that won’t even be raised externally for months or years. I find that for research directions where GDM holds a firm moat, the bureaucracy also happens to be generally better than areas with lots of fierce competition. For what it's worth, I think it’s definitely possible (and good!) to do very impactful research on these topics at other labs or academia, but the research just won’t be quite at *the* bleeding edge.
2) Hot take and just my personal opinion: if AGI first comes out of one of OpenAI, Anthropic, XAI, and GDM, the most societally beneficial outcome is if AGI comes out of GDM. Not necessarily because of the actual technical progress or the talent, but because of incentive alignment and organizational structure. For all the BigCo problems GDM has, it also benefits from BigCo advantages: GDM is structurally stable and has the luxury of being more insulated from short-term decision making pressures that are extremely intense. No matter how idealistic and mission-driven AGI labs are, the realities of a hyper-competitive AI research and product landscape mean that thoughtful and responsible fundamental research gets influenced by fundraising hype, product shipping timelines, and marketing clout-chasing. This influence is notoriously pervasive, and drowns out any noble attempts to protect the research mission (see: concentration of power, deprioritization of safety/alignment research, accelerated shipping timelines of sometimes immature products, board changes). I claim that the GDM AGI research mission is significantly less affected by these factors than other labs.
There are of course many areas where GDM could improve in a lot! Points about compensation and bureaucracy are very valid. But for doing cool bleeding-edge research with fun smart people for AGI with a positive social impact, I think GDM is still an amazing place to be.

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
The promise of robot foundation models is that they're one of the strongest approaches to enabling robust generalization to novel in-the-wild scenarios. The new π-0.5 release shows great progress towards generalizing to realistic household tasks! Congrats to the whole @physical_int team on the milestone.
Some quick thoughts below:
What I liked
- π-0.5 embraces the VLA ethos a lot more than π-0. The point of a VLA is to leverage the full power of the VLM backbone to transfer semantic and spatial knowledge from (1) broad internet knowledge and (2) diverse data distributions, including data not from your specific robot in your specific target deployment scenario. π-0.5 expands the scope of "robot pre-training" to include co-training with diverse datasets, in contrast with just considering "robot pre-training" to be cross-embodiment training on robot data alone. Training on multimodal internet data, on robot non-action datasets, on multi-environment datasets -- these are all very important ingredients to robot learning!
- I really like baking subtask planning into both pre-training, post-training, and inference. A robot foundation model should not just memorize low-level control properties or only spit out robot actions, but it should also retain and transfer high-level task planning and semantic knowledge. Using the subtask planning chain of thought makes a lot of sense, and it's great to see it outperform treating subtask planning as an implicit auxiliary task. In RT-2, we explored a variant which does autoregressive planning and then action prediction, but π-0.5 did a great job at thoroughly ablating this and showing benefits (Fig. 13). This just makes sense, especially for long-horizon autonomous task chaining. We've come so far from SayCan days, where such orchestration required a separate Q-network and a separate LLM planner.
- The analysis on the individual contribution of each data source (web data, cross-embodiment, multi-environment) was very insightful. There's been a lively debate in the robotics community on the role/importance of cross-embodiment data vs. visual diversity, and it's great to have another data point (at scale) -- clearly having neither performs very poorly (Fig. 10). The updated pre-training => post-training spectrum also starts to set up a coarse-to-fine process which better reflects foundation modeling best practices, where more relevant data is emphasized in post-training (overlapping more with the deployment environment, such as sharing the same robot or environment) compared to more generic datasets (still useful but not 100% immediately relevant, such as cross-embodiment data).
- The production quality of the blog post and teaser videos was mindblowing. I am still on the fence about the difficulty of the evaluation scenario (more on that below), but this release is unequivocally inspiring and is a great reminder why general-purpose mobile manipulation is going to be the unlock that enables ubiquitous robots in society. Breakdancing humanoids are great, but the π-0.5 story -- just driving around to new homes and carrying in a robot which works out of the box -- really highlights the scenarios and breakthroughs that will make general robotics helpful and delightful for everyday humans in home environments.
What I'm looking forward to in the future
- The main tasks studied for in-the-wild evals are all variants of fairly simple pick and place tasks (dishes in sink, items in drawer, laundry in basket), where ordering doesn't really matter and there aren't that many choices or branching factors. This makes the results from instruction following (Fig. 11) and high-level inference (Fig. 13) a bit inconsistent to me: if the policy is very good at following language specifications, then why is the policy significantly worse at long-horizon task completion when guided with human subtasks instead of model-proposed subtasks? In many previous works, human-provided subtask steering is often an upper bound oracle (in fact, this was the motivation for this baseline in the paper), so it's very strange that π-0.5 regresses when steered by a human, especially when the subtasks seem quite simple (for example, mode-selecting which dish to pick up first or which shirt to pick first).
- None of the long-horizon tasks seem to have any dexterous subtasks or bottlenecks. One exception is perhaps the "Make Bed" task, but that was only tested in the lab Mock Home setting, which I presume is easier than in-the-wild homes. I believe that the main challenge for the Real Home evals is background and object generalization (as opposed to action generalization), which from prior works we know to be some of the easier axes of generalization. To be fair, these evals introduced significant distribution shifts to these axes, in a very realistically-motivated way; but we have known that models leveraging strong vision priors (via VLM backbones or pretrained visual representations) can also be quite powerful at tackling drastic visual and object generalization.
- The policies seem to be quite slow; most videos were 5x or 10x sped up. This is in part due to the impressive long-horizon nature of the rollouts (5-10 minutes!), but also highlights that each pick or place subtask takes up to a minute, which is a lot slower than prior works, including VLAs on dexterous bi-arm platforms.
Overall, I am super impressed as usual with the execution of the whole Physical Intelligence team. It's awesome to see π-0.5 enter the "true" VLA era with much more heterogeneous data distributions and corresponding focus on robust generalization.

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
ICYMI: robotics is quickly taking over mindshare in the AI research community!
The Robot Learning Workshop at #ICLR2025 saw unprecedented turnout, ~2x previous robotics workshops at mainstream AI conferences. The next frontier for AGI is in the physical world.
Quoting @Andrey__Kolobov
A week after our 🤖 7th Robot Learning Workshop @ #ICLR2025 🤖 in 🇸🇬, the surreal feeling is still with me.
300 people in the room consistently throughout the day, and at times way more, making it difficult to enter. This easily surpassed the attendance of any robotics-themed workshop at any prior AI/ML conference like NeurIPS, ICML, and ICLR, as well as our own, organizers', estimates by 2x. Despite many US-based community members being unable to come due to funding and visa uncertainty. Despite workshops on hot topics like foundation models and agentic AI for science happening in parallel.
I have no surefire explanation for this. My impression is that robot learning is still a relatively fringe topic at AI venues, including ICLR, and ICLR isn't even the largest of them. Being close to the bustling robotics scene in Asia has certainly helped. So have the demos by @boosterobotics and @Frodobots - driving a small car on the streets of Mauritius 🇲🇺 from a seat in Singapore 🇸🇬 and seeing humanoids mingle with the audience and kicking the ⚽️ around has really spiced up the workshop (see @frodobots' coverage at the end👇)! The panel, contributed and invited talks - definitely. There was a lot new to be said 6 months after CoRL. But I also see this increased interest as the beginning of a recognition that the problems studied by the robot learning community are central to AI research at large.
Either way, it felt like magic🪄. I hope it continues in the years to come.
Mad props to the invited speakers and panelists @chris_j_paxton, @davsca1, @jixing24, @chelseabfinn, David Hsu, @animesh_garg, Sandy Huang, @ColinearDevin, @Ed__Johns, @nireshdravin, and Chaoyi Li, to all the authors of the contributed papers, to our sponsors @MSFTResearch and @frodobots, and, of course, to @boosterobotics and @frodobots again for their demos.

summary:
Very impressive Tesla autonomy update for manipulation! 🤖👋
There are a handful of high-leverage bets in robotics + AI that are risky but would have transformative impact if they’re unlocked, and Tesla’s latest update shows some progress on one of them: transferring knowledge from human interaction videos directly to low-level robot control.
A year ago, there was a lot of chatter around Tesla’s strict hiring requirements for teleoperators (ie. matching the physical dimensions of the robot, so that morion targeting from human to robot via motion capture suits / exoskeletons would be easier). But in the brief sample we see at the end of this new demo video, the 1st person human videos clearly are much less instrumented than Tesla’s previous progress; there are no VR controllers, no bulky gloves with IMU/wiring attached. Clearly, there’s been some progress on learning from “noisier” human data, akin to moving from LiDAR based AV to vision-only AV.
One interesting detail I noticed: there are some colored gloves in the egocentric video at the end. Not sure if these contain sensors, are helpful for data augmentation (ie. domain randomization to make transferring from human hand appearance to robot hand appearance easier), or for more visual diversity.
Congrats to the whole @Tesla_Optimus team @julianibarz @_milankovac_ @mendonca_rl @mihdalal @Yi__Li!

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
The most significant impact of superhuman AI may not be economic or technological, but spiritual.
How do leaders of faith view AI today, and how will this relationship evolve as it reaches critical thresholds of intelligence and ubiquity?
On one hand, it's easy to frame strong AI as heretical. Is it not the ultimate hubris, a modern Babel, to imagine that the infinite depth of the human spirit can be distilled into a finite set of parameters etched onto silicon? The very idea of the supervised learning objective — Imago Dei, of cloning the human mind by observing its external effects — seems to defy the sanctity of the soul. If a person, in their entirety, could be losslessly compressed based on material attributes alone, what would that imply about the role of faith in explaining the unique, irreducible nature of the individual? Faith is meant to address the indescribable. But what happens if AI begins to describe everything?
On the other hand, perhaps superhuman AI is an Avatar, a a new manifestation of the divine. Just as the physical universe marches toward higher entropy, perhaps religion is the spiritual process by which conscious beings ascend to higher planes of understanding. If a higher power initiated a grand adventure for intelligent life to discover its place in the cosmos, could AI be the next chapter in this journey toward enlightenment? Could self-improving superhuman AI be the next physical embodiment of a deity, a Bodhisattva come to shepherd us to the future? Just as prophets and deities have walked among us before, perhaps they will again; not as flesh and bone, but as glass and silicon.
Or maybe superhuman AI is neither the end nor the beginning, but simply a means. It could be an accelerating medium, a tool to deepen our connection with the holy. AI systems have already digested more theological doctrine and scripture in their original languages than all devoted acolytes of all faiths, combined. Used as a tool, AI could contextualize religious orthodoxy while simultaneously acting as a scalable and effective evangelist, enabling people of all creeds to better understand and live their faith.
Faith has always been a cornerstone of the human condition, but it will face its most formidable evolutionary test yet in superhuman AI. This confrontation will inevitably transform spiritual traditions, forcing us to ask whether they will be shattered by our own creation or remade into something entirely new.

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
It is very difficult to properly convey “zero-shot generalization”, it’s a very overloaded and overabused term these days! But let me try to add some color to why so many of my colleagues have been so shocked at what the Gemini Robotics 1.5 VLA has been doing… 🎨
The whole point of a VLA is to guarantee positive transfer by leveraging internet data to learn capabilities that you don’t need to cover with expensive real-world data collection on your robot. And this kind of works! We’ve now seen this positive transfer appear many times as semantic or visual policy generalization: understanding new visual-lingual concepts like “Taylor Swift” or “healthy snack” or being more robust to background and lighting changes.
But *motion level generalization* has remained elusive. Back in 2023 with OXE/RT-X, we thought that naively pre-training a VLA on massively cross-embodied robot data mixtures might give us some of this right off the bat. We searched extensively for motion level improvements. For example, while our Google robot had never connected “pouring” task data, we knew that other robots had seen this data. But despite extensive evaluations, the main gains we found were semantic: understanding concepts like “next to” or “on top of”.
In 2025, many *post-training* methods now aim to showcase motion-level transfer (ie. across different types of tabletop manipulators with different kinematics or from egocentric human to humanoid) by explicitly retargeting. But the dream, I would argue, has always been to discover a general motion-generalization approach which is extendable to *pre-training*.
With the Gemini Robotics 1.5 VLA, we pushed hard to make a dent in this problem, but we were still very puzzled at how strong the initial evaluations were. We thought that there must be a bug, some data leakage. But after thorough debugging and validation, we began to believe the results. A *pre-trained checkpoint*, trained on disjoint data distributions on multiple robot platforms (Aloha, Bi-arm Franka, Apollo Humanoid) was showcasing motion level transfer! Despite the Aloha *never* seeing a tool hanging task (reaching at that height and horizontal depth with very specific asymmetric motion needed for a precise hang), it was able to repeatably succeed. Same story for Aloha to Apollo, for Bi-arm Franka to Aloha, all the bi-directional pairs.
To be honest, the results still feel shocking. It feels like the very early days of RT-2 when we first started seeing promising signs of life with the first large-scale VLA training run. I have more questions than answers right now, but this is where some of the science and the real fun begins 🚀
Quoting @bousmalis
You have to watch this! For years now, I've been looking for signs of nontrivial zero-shot transfer across seen embodiments. When I saw the Alohas unhang tools from a wall used only on our Frankas I knew we had it! Gemini Robotics 1.5 is the first VLA to achieve such transfer!!
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/1973357450536386560/img/e2a5ELrNKXubIzD3.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/1973357450536386560/vid/avc1/480x270/GZeIWDkMYR1pGwuK.mp4?tag=14

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
There is a simple but universal reality that more are beginning to appreciate: the physical world is rate limiting.
Whether you believe that AGI is imminent, that digital tool-using agents will completely disrupt knowledge work, that abstract scientific and creative work will be automated, or even that AI is fundamentally not a normal technology…
…an unavoidable fact is that real-world wall time cannot be hacked or gamed. Spinning up more GPU clusters will not accelerate the laws of physics. You cannot CoT or search your way through latency-critical decisions. There is no `env.reset()` for physical systems operating in real-world scenarios. There is no escaping the conundrum that the two elastic ingredients which power the Bitter Lesson, compute and search, must confront the inelastic limiting reactant that is reality.
The problem itself, of course, gets combinatorially harder the more dimensions you add: extending the time horizon of physical problems, adding precision and accuracy requirements, increasing complexity and performance expectations, evolving the amount of real-world contact needed (from freeform flight to wheeled navigation to legged locomotion to industrial manipulation to multi-fingered dexterous hands). Adding any one of these dimensions, let alone several, increases the problem difficulty by at least an order of magnitude.
Moravec’s Paradox speaks to the comparative cognitive difficulty of tasks which come naturally to humans, but the structural and economic difficulties of real-world messiness are just as important. Just as there is a hardware lottery which has resulted in a self-selecting cycle of algorithms developing based on chip properties, there has also been an application lottery which has driven immense AI progress on applications where research and scaling are limited primarily by smart algorithms or diligent engineering. If you feel like a problem can be solved with just a dash of ingenuity and code, then you can bet that many other smart researchers feel the same, and more likely than not, that problem will indeed be accelerated and solved soon.
But the real world is not that. Everywhere you look, the compounding effects of physical rate limitation rear their heads, from real-world hardware iteration cycle times, infrastructure, and supply chains to large-scale data collection and evaluation, massive economic capitalization requirements, and long and uncertain timelines for value capture. The real world is hard. We are starting to see various realizations of this concept (albeit sometimes conflated with geopolitics) with commendable pushes towards re-industrialization, hard tech, general purpose physical AGI, and humanoids.
And I am glad for that. I can think of no problem which is more important, interesting, or novel. Because for any problem that touches reality, no matter how lightly, that touchpoint will always become the bottleneck. In a world of so many uncertainties, of this at least I am sure of: physical AGI will be the final frontier of AI as a whole. We are still so, so early. But the future is bright, and it will be a future built, tested, and ultimately measured against the physical world.

title: Ted Xiao (@xiao_ted)
summary:
Compelling advances in scaling laws for robotics from @GeneralistAI! Scaling laws are without a doubt one of the key components that enabled the rapid hyperscaling of language model pre-training over the past years. Establishing predictive scaling laws would be a watershed moment for general purpose robotics, and the recent analysis from Generalist is some of the most promising I've seen so far. But, there are some nuances that I'd like to raise; think of these ideas as an open bounty for high-impact future work 🚀
#1 Language modeling has found that scaling laws measured on metrics like training loss [1] or monorepo perplexity [2] provide accurate approximations of observed downstream evaluation performance. However, an open secret in robotics is that offline metrics, such as training or validation loss, exact-match token accuracy, or open-loop offline action MSE, have been notoriously uncorrelated with real-world close-loop performance! Reliable offline evaluation metrics have been a holy grail for robotics that remains unsolved [3]. Oftentimes, model checkpoints with higher validation loss may actually result in better end-to-end performance in the real world; this makes checkpoint selection, model iteration, and power law analysis extremely difficult. This has many reasons, but an intuitive illustration is that robot policies often have very jagged properties in terms of their learned behavior: if model A fits the training distribution extremely well but is brittle and sometimes makes rare but catastrophic errors, it may exhibit much lower action MSE compared to a model B which is slightly worse on all states but never makes unrecoverable errors. There are many such considerations when comparing offline metrics with online closed-loop rollouts: compounding errors, model brittleness, in-distribution vs. out-of-distribution generalization performance. But even offline closed-loop evaluation is difficult, and leveraging simulation [4] or world models [5] for evaluation are an open research problem. Generalist proposed scaling laws across dataset size and model scale, as measured against validation loss during a post-training phase on target tasks; while an interesting result at a larger scale than previous work ([6], [7], [8]), this result is not as convincing as I would like because while one can argue that the proposed power laws are true, it is unclear if they are meaningful power laws because the correlation between validation loss and real-world performance has been highly dependent on the policy type, model class, task complexity, and deployment situation.
#2 Scaling laws in language modeling have been immensely useful during pretraining laddering (where ideas are explored at smaller scales and can be used to make critical decisions for larger hero runs) because of their predictive power. The trends and slopes of metrics like compute efficiency when measuring specific domains like code or Wikipedia oftentimes accurately measure how general model intelligence will improve on other tasks as varied as MMLU or GPQA. However, in robotics, scaling law analysis is overfit to a single embodiment on a single set of tasks; it does not translate to a universal predictive scaling law to apply to other robots or other scenarios! A derived scaling law for the relationship between model size, FLOPs, and hours of demonstrations needed to solve Task A on an ALOHA may not necessarily tell you much at all about the scaling law for Task B on a humanoid. In robotics, scaling laws are often time only backwards-looking: if you were to re-do the same project under the exact same requirements, you could have saved X amount of time by collecting less data / training a smaller model. But it may not tell you anything about the next task or next environment you deploy in.
Overall, I am excited and impressed by the scale of Generalist's immense data collection operations, the gorgeously smooth and performant model behaviors, and the scientifically rigorous push to make real progress on scaling laws for robotics. The team has been cooking! In the future, I look forward to extensions to this scaling analysis (from Generalist or the community!) for (A) moving beyond validation loss to more trustworthy performance measurements and (B) showing predictive power of truly universal scaling laws as opposed to backwards looking task and embodiment specific scaling laws. These are hard problems, and I look forward to seeing progress on this front!
